title: The system: game build and patch distribution built around an object store
caption: CI uploads only the chunks the store doesn't have yet, a manifest says which chunks make a version, and players fetch what they miss from a CDN that almost never reaches the bucket.

steps.text: CI finishes a 60 GB build. CI splits every file into content-defined chunks of about 8 MB, names each one by the SHA-256 of its bytes, and sends the publisher only the list of hashes.
Most chunks are identical to the previous version's. The publisher hands out presigned PUT URLs only for the new hashes, and CI uploads those straight to the bucket: a few GB, not 60.
The publisher writes the manifest (every file, and the ordered chunk hashes it is made of) to the manifest DB. At release time, release control points 'live' at the new version.
Each launcher asks the patch API for the live manifest, compares it with the one it installed, and lists the chunks it lacks.

It downloads those chunks from the nearest CDN edge by hash. Misses go to the origin shield, which turns many concurrent misses for one chunk into one GET to the bucket. Chunk keys never change, so they are cached for a year.
Lifecycle rules move chunks used only by old builds to a cold tier, and the shield reports origin load and hit ratio to monitoring.

scenarios.name: Patch day
scenarios.summary: Millions of launchers want the same few thousand new chunks within an hour. The CDN carries the load; the bucket sees each chunk only a handful of times.

steps.text: At release, millions of launchers fetch the manifest within minutes. It is small and the same for everyone, so the patch API serves it from cache.
Every player needs the same new chunks. Edges that were pre-warmed answer at once; cold edges send their first misses to the shield.
The shield collapses concurrent misses: thousands of edge requests for one chunk become one origin GET.
Origin load stays flat while CDN egress climbs to many Tbps. The dashboard to watch is shield hit ratio, not bucket throughput.

scenarios.name: Manifest DB down
scenarios.summary: The database is on the control path, not the download path: players keep patching, only publishing stops.

steps.text: The manifest DB's primary fails during a failover window.
A version's manifest never changes once committed, so the patch API keeps serving the cached live manifest.
Chunk downloads never touched the database and carry on through the CDN.
What stops is publishing: new builds can't commit a manifest until the replica is promoted. CI uploads can still run, since the chunks are just objects.

scenarios.name: Roll back a bad patch
scenarios.summary: A patch crashes on launch. Rolling back is a pointer change, not a cache purge: the old version's chunks are still in the store and still cached.

steps.text: Crash reports spike an hour after release. An operator points 'live' back at the previous version.
The patch API's cached pointer expires within a minute; launchers see the old manifest again.
Launchers that already updated download only the chunks that differ, most of them still on the edges. Nothing needs purging because no key was overwritten.
This works only if the previous version's chunks are still hot: lifecycle rules keep the last few live versions out of the cold tier.
